question: What is the primary function of antigens found on the surface of red blood cells?

options.A: Act as identification markers for the immune system
options.B: Transport oxygen molecules to peripheral tissues
options.C: Maintain the structural integrity of cell membranes
options.D: Regulate blood pH levels during metabolic activity

explanation: Antigens are chemical structures on cell surfaces that the immune system uses to distinguish self from non-self. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h1)

question: What triggers the production of specific antibodies in a patient's plasma?

options.A: Exposure to unfamiliar red blood cell antigens
options.B: Prolonged exposure to high ambient temperatures
options.C: Elevation of white blood cell counts during infection
options.D: Depletion of iron stores in the bone marrow

explanation: Antibodies develop in the plasma when the immune system encounters foreign antigens that it does not recognize as part of the body. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which antibodies are naturally present in the plasma of a person with blood group A?
explanation: Blood group A red cells carry A antigens, so the plasma develops naturally occurring anti-B antibodies to prevent reaction against self-tissues. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h2)

question: Why is an individual with blood group AB referred to as a universal plasma donor?

options.A: Their immune system never produces any antibodies throughout life
options.B: Their plasma contains no ABO antibodies to attack recipient cells
options.C: Their blood contains the highest concentration of clotting factors
options.D: Their red blood cells lack both A and B surface antigens

explanation: Because group AB plasma lacks both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, it will not cause agglutination when infused into recipients of other ABO groups. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary trigger for an Rh-negative individual to develop anti-D antibodies?

options.A: Undergoing severe bacterial infections in childhood
options.B: Prior exposure to Rh-positive red blood cells
options.C: Consuming foods rich in inorganic iron compounds
options.D: Inheriting specific genetic traits from both parents

explanation: Anti-D antibodies are not naturally occurring and only develop after the immune system is sensitized by exposure to Rh-positive blood. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h3)

question: A primigravida patient who is Rh-negative gives birth to an Rh-positive baby without receiving postnatal prophylaxis. What is the primary risk during a subsequent pregnancy with another Rh-positive fetus?

options.A: Immediate maternal rejection of the placenta during the first trimester
options.B: The mother developing sudden acute hemolytic transfusion reactions
options.C: Maternal antibodies crossing the placenta and destroying fetal red cells
options.D: Complete suppression of fetal bone marrow platelet production

explanation: Sensitization from the first pregnancy causes the mother to produce IgG anti-D antibodies that can cross the placenta in future pregnancies and cause hemolytic disease of the newborn. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h3)

question: What macroscopic sign indicates a positive reaction during standard blood typing laboratory tests?

options.A: A distinct change in the sample's color to bright green
options.B: Complete dissolution of the cell mixture
options.D: Agglutination of the red blood cells

explanation: Agglutination, or clumping, occurs when antibodies bind to matching antigens on red blood cells, indicating a positive test result. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why is reverse blood grouping performed alongside forward grouping in the laboratory?

options.A: To screen the patient's blood for hidden bacterial pathogens
options.B: To measure the exact hemoglobin concentration in the sample
options.C: To confirm cell typing results by checking plasma antibodies
options.D: To determine the total volume of blood available for transfusion

explanation: Reverse grouping checks the patient's serum for expected antibodies, acting as an essential cross-check against the forward cell typing results. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h4)

question: What are the two primary components mixed together during a standard blood cross-match procedure?

options.A: Recipient red blood cells and donor plasma
options.B: Recipient serum and donor red blood cells
options.C: Donor serum and commercial anti-D antisera
options.D: Recipient platelets and whole donor blood

explanation: A cross-match tests the recipient's serum against donor red blood cells to ensure no unexpected recipient antibodies will destroy the donor cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h5)

question: When is it clinically acceptable to issue uncrossmatched blood for an emergency transfusion?

options.A: When the patient belongs exclusively to blood group AB positive
options.B: When the hospital blood bank has ran out of testing reagents
options.C: When the patient requests a rapid transfusion to leave the hospital
options.D: When acute hemorrhagic shock poses an immediate threat to life

explanation: In life-threatening emergencies where waiting for a full cross-match would cause patient death, uncrossmatched type O blood is issued. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is evaluated during a major cross-match procedure?

options.A: Recipient platelets against donor clotting factors
options.B: Donor serum against recipient red blood cells
options.C: Donor white cells against recipient immunoglobulins
options.D: Recipient serum against donor red blood cells

explanation: The major cross-match ensures that antibodies in the recipient's plasma will not attack and hemolyze the incoming donor red blood cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h6)

question: Why has routine performance of the minor cross-match largely diminished in contemporary blood banking?

options.A: Discovery that minor cross-matching causes severe allergic reactions
options.B: Complete elimination of antibody screening requirements in donor centers
options.C: Development of synthetic artificial blood substitutes that lack plasma
options.D: Widespread use of packed red cells with minimal residual donor plasma

explanation: Because modern components contain very little donor plasma, testing donor serum against recipient cells is no longer necessary as a routine measure. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is the maximum recommended time limit for completing a single unit of blood transfusion from the moment it leaves the blood bank?
explanation: Blood must be infused within four hours to prevent bacterial multiplication in blood products kept at room temperature. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h7)

question: Why must a nurse remain with the patient during the first 15 minutes of a blood transfusion?

options.A: Patients require continuous psychological reassurance throughout
options.B: The infusion pump demands constant manual calibration during setup
options.C: Intravenous lines frequently dislodge right after starting the flow
options.D: Most severe acute transfusion reactions occur early in the infusion

explanation: Severe acute hemolytic and allergic reactions typically manifest within the first few minutes or after the initial 50 mL of blood is infused. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is the immediate first action a nurse must take if a patient shows signs of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Slow the infusion rate down to half
options.B: Collect a repeat set of vital signs

explanation: Stopping the transfusion immediately prevents any further infusion of incompatible blood cells and limits the severity of the reaction. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h8)

question: A patient receiving a unit of packed red blood cells develops severe dyspnea, hypertension, jugular venous distension, and crackles in both lung fields halfway through the infusion. Which complication is most likely occurring?
explanation: Hypertension, dyspnea, and pulmonary crackles during or soon after transfusion are hallmark signs of fluid overload (TACO). [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h8)
